introduction: Helena, a physician's daughter living in a noble household, loves the young Count Bertram despite the gulf between their ranks. Her father's medical legacy gives her a chance to approach the King of France, whose illness has defeated his doctors. But royal favour cannot guarantee affection, and Bertram's ambitions lead toward the wars in Italy. Across France and Florence, the play tests noble reputation against conduct, sets practical ingenuity against proud resistance, and follows two women negotiating the demands men make upon them.

fullSynopsis.text: After her father, the physician Gerard de Narbon, dies, Helena remains under the protection of the Countess of Rossillon. She secretly loves the Countess's son Bertram, who considers her far beneath him in rank. When he leaves to attend the sick King of France, Helena resolves to follow with a remedy inherited from her father. The Countess discovers her love and supports the journey. Helena persuades the despairing King to try her treatment, staking her life on success and asking, if she cures him, to choose a husband from his subjects.

The cure succeeds, and Helena chooses Bertram. He rejects the idea of marrying a poor physician's daughter, but the King defends her worth and compels his ward to submit. Bertram undergoes the marriage ceremony while privately determining never to consummate it. Encouraged by his boastful companion Parolles, he sends Helena home and escapes to the Florentine war. Lafew has already recognized Parolles as a hollow pretender, but Bertram continues to trust him. Helena's obedient farewell receives neither the affection nor even the parting kiss she seeks.

At Rossillon, Helena receives Bertram's declaration that she can call him husband only when she possesses his treasured family ring and carries his child: conditions he presents as impossible. The Countess condemns her son and embraces Helena as her child. Believing her presence keeps Bertram in danger abroad, Helena leaves on pilgrimage. In Florence she meets a widow and her daughter Diana, whom Bertram is pursuing. Helena reveals herself to the widow and proposes that Diana demand his ring and arrange a secret encounter, with Helena taking Diana's place in the dark.

Meanwhile, two French lords undertake to expose Parolles by encouraging his promise to recover a lost drum. Their soldiers seize and blindfold him, speaking invented foreign languages so that he believes himself captured by enemies. To save his life, he offers military intelligence and slanders his comrades before Bertram and the lords. When they unmask him, he accepts that his career as a captain is over, yet resolves to survive his disgrace. Diana obtains Bertram's ring and requires silence during their supposed meeting; the encounter with Helena occurs offstage.

With peace concluded and Helena reported dead, Bertram prepares to return to France. Helena, alive and conscious of the report, travels with Diana and the widow to seek the King's help. At Rossillon, Lafew and the Countess favour Bertram's proposed marriage to Lafew's daughter. The King forgives Bertram, but recognizes a ring Bertram offers as a token for the new match: it was his gift to Helena. Bertram's false account of acquiring it, together with his hatred of Helena, raises suspicion that her reported death conceals a crime.

Diana petitions the King for justice, produces Bertram's ancestral ring and exposes his promises and evasions. Parolles confirms his role as intermediary. Diana sends for Helena, who presents the ring and Bertram's letter and declares herself pregnant by him. Bertram asks pardon and promises lasting love if the explanation is made clear; Helena accepts their union on the same test of truth. The King asks to hear the whole story and offers Diana a husband and dowry. Lafew promises the disgraced Parolles a place in his household, while the epilogue asks the audience's applause to complete the happy ending.

acts.label: ACT I
acts.summary: Bertram leaves his recently widowed mother to become the King's ward at Paris, accompanied by Lafew and Parolles. Helena, the daughter of a dead physician and the Countess's dependent, reveals that her grief chiefly concerns her love for Bertram, whose social rank seems to put marriage beyond her reach. Her sharp exchange with Parolles about virginity also exposes her awareness of his cowardice and dishonesty. At court, the ailing King welcomes Bertram for his father's sake and permits French gentlemen to serve in the Italian war. After her steward reports Helena's secret, the Countess questions her sympathetically. Helena confesses her love and explains her plan to use her father's medicine to cure the King. The Countess supplies permission, means and encouragement for her journey.

acts.label: ACT II
acts.summary: The King initially refuses Helena's remedy, but she persuades him to risk an experiment and pledges her life against failure. In return for a cure, he promises her the husband she chooses from his subjects. Restored to health, he presents his young lords, and Helena chooses Bertram. Bertram openly despises her low birth and denies any willingness to love her. The King counters that virtue creates honour, offers her wealth and title, and forces Bertram to accept the marriage. Lafew repeatedly punctures Parolles's military pretensions, without shaking Bertram's trust. After the ceremony, Parolles encourages Bertram to escape to war rather than share his wife's bed. Bertram sends Helena home with letters, disguising his permanent rejection as a temporary absence and refusing her request for a farewell kiss.

acts.label: ACT III
acts.summary: Bertram serves Florence and receives command of its cavalry. At home, the Countess learns that he has abandoned Helena; his letter makes acceptance conditional on her obtaining his family ring and bearing his child. The Countess takes Helena's side, but Helena blames herself for driving him into danger and leaves as a pilgrim. In Florence she meets the widow who lodges pilgrims and Diana, the daughter whom Bertram has been trying to seduce through Parolles. Concealing her identity at first, Helena learns of his pursuit. She then secures the widow's help with a plan: Diana will ask for Bertram's ring and promise an encounter, while Helena will replace her in bed. Separately, French officers persuade Bertram to test Parolles by letting him attempt to recover a lost drum, preparing a sham enemy capture to reveal his character.

acts.label: ACT IV
acts.summary: Soldiers posing as foreigners capture Parolles as he prepares excuses for failing to recover the drum. Blindfolded, he immediately offers to betray his army. Diana challenges Bertram's vows against his duty to his wife, obtains his ancestral ring, and appoints a silent midnight meeting at which another ring will pass to him. Bertram later believes he has enjoyed Diana, while Helena speaks of his unknowingly embracing the wife he hates. Before Bertram and the French lords, the captive Parolles gives intelligence, invents scandal about his comrades and exposes his contempt for Bertram. Released and disgraced, he resolves to live without his captain's title. Peace is concluded, and a report of Helena's death allows Bertram to plan his homecoming. Helena takes Diana and the widow toward the King; at Rossillon, Lafew proposes his daughter as Bertram's next wife.

acts.label: ACT V
acts.summary: Helena misses the King at Marseilles and sends a petition ahead to Rossillon. There, the needy Parolles appeals to Lafew, who promises him food and later a place at home. The King forgives Bertram and approves a match with Lafew's daughter, until Bertram produces the ring once given to Helena. His denials arouse suspicion concerning her supposed death. Diana arrives claiming his marriage promise and displaying his family ring; Bertram first slanders her, then admits his pursuit, while Parolles supplies awkward confirmation. Diana's riddling testimony brings threats of imprisonment before the widow produces Helena alive. Helena displays the ring and letter and announces that she carries Bertram's child. He asks pardon and promises love if the account is proved. The King defers a full explanation, offering Diana a husband and dowry while the reunion is received with joy.

framing.label: Epilogue
framing.summary: The performer who has played the King becomes a petitioner for the audience's approval. He makes the declaration that all has ended well depend on their contentment and asks for applause in exchange for the players' continuing efforts to please.
